title: Hemophilia
description: Hemophilia A and B in children: X-linked inheritance, labs, hemarthrosis, factor replacement and DDAVP, bleeding precautions, intracranial bleeding, and safe activity.
keyPoints: X-linked recessive: affected males, carrier females. Hemophilia A = factor VIII deficiency; hemophilia B = factor IX deficiency.
Labs: prolonged PTT, normal PT, normal platelet count; low factor VIII or IX activity.
Hemarthrosis is the most common bleed (warmth, pain, stiffness, swelling). Repeated bleeds cause permanent joint damage.
Treat bleeds with factor replacement plus RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation). DDAVP for mild hemophilia A.
Avoid IM injections, rectal temperatures, aspirin, and NSAIDs. Use acetaminophen for pain.
Head injury with headache, vomiting, irritability, or lethargy = possible intracranial bleed; give factor and seek emergency care.
Encourage noncontact exercise like swimming; avoid contact sports. Wear a medical alert ID.

questions.stem: A mother who is a carrier of hemophilia A and a father without hemophilia ask about their children's risk. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Each son has a 50% chance of hemophilia, and each daughter a 50% chance of being a carrier.
options.rationale: Correct. Hemophilia is X-linked recessive. A carrier mother passes the affected X to half her children: affected sons, carrier daughters.

options.text: All sons will have hemophilia, and all daughters will be carriers.
options.rationale: Only children who inherit the affected X are affected or carriers; each son has a 50%, not 100%, chance.

options.text: Daughters have a 50% chance of severe hemophilia, and sons will be carriers.
options.rationale: Daughters receive a normal X from the father and are carriers, not affected; males with the affected X have hemophilia rather than being carriers.

options.text: Only the first-born son is at risk, and later children will be unaffected.
options.rationale: Each pregnancy carries the same independent risk.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency, about 80-85%) and hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency, Christmas disease) are X-linked recessive. Males are affected; females are usually carriers. About one-third of cases arise from new mutations.

questions.stem: An 11-month-old boy is evaluated for a large bruise on the thigh after crawling and prolonged bleeding after a heel stick. Which laboratory results are consistent with hemophilia?

options.text: Prolonged PT, normal PTT, low platelet count
options.rationale: A low platelet count suggests thrombocytopenia, and a prolonged PT suggests a different factor or liver problem.

options.text: Normal PT, prolonged PTT, normal platelet count
options.rationale: Correct. Factors VIII and IX are part of the intrinsic pathway measured by the PTT. Platelets and the extrinsic pathway (PT) are normal.

options.text: Normal PT, normal PTT, low platelet count
options.rationale: This pattern suggests immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).

options.text: Prolonged PT and PTT with low fibrinogen
options.rationale: This pattern suggests disseminated intravascular coagulation.

questions.explanation: Hemophilia labs: prolonged PTT, normal PT, normal platelet count and bleeding time, and low factor VIII or IX activity. Diagnosis is confirmed by factor assay.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with hemophilia A falls off a bike and reports a painful, warm, swollen right knee. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Administer the prescribed factor VIII concentrate.
options.rationale: Correct. Factor replacement is the priority treatment for a hemarthrosis and should be given as soon as possible to stop the bleeding.

options.text: Apply heat and encourage range-of-motion exercises.
options.rationale: Heat increases bleeding; exercise is avoided during an acute bleed.

options.text: Give ibuprofen for pain.
options.rationale: NSAIDs impair platelet function and increase bleeding.

options.text: Wrap the knee and have the child walk on it to prevent stiffness.
options.rationale: Weight bearing during an acute joint bleed worsens bleeding and damage.

questions.explanation: Hemarthrosis is the most common bleeding site in hemophilia. Treat promptly with factor replacement plus RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation). Repeated joint bleeds cause chronic arthropathy and disability.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a 6-year-old with an acute bleed into the elbow joint. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Immobilize and rest the joint
options.rationale: Rest limits further bleeding.

options.text: Apply ice for short periods
options.rationale: Cold promotes vasoconstriction and reduces pain and swelling.

options.text: Elevate the arm above heart level
options.rationale: Elevation reduces blood flow to the area.

options.text: Give aspirin for pain
options.rationale: Aspirin inhibits platelet function and increases bleeding.

options.text: Apply gentle compression with an elastic wrap
options.rationale: Compression helps limit bleeding into the joint.

options.text: Begin vigorous physical therapy right away
options.rationale: Passive and active exercises begin after the acute bleed is controlled, usually within 48 hours, to prevent stiffness.

questions.explanation: RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) plus factor replacement treats bleeds. Use acetaminophen or opioids for pain, never aspirin or NSAIDs. Physical therapy begins once bleeding has stopped.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with severe hemophilia A fell and hit his head 2 hours ago. He is now irritable, vomiting, and says his head hurts. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Viral gastroenteritis
options.rationale: Vomiting alone could be gastroenteritis, but combined with a recent head injury, headache, and irritability in hemophilia, a bleed must be assumed.

options.text: Expected behavior after a minor fall
options.rationale: Any head trauma in hemophilia is treated as a potential emergency.

options.text: Intracranial hemorrhage
options.rationale: Correct. Headache, vomiting, irritability, lethargy, or changes in level of consciousness after head trauma suggest an intracranial bleed, the leading cause of death from bleeding in hemophilia. Factor is given immediately.

options.text: Hemarthrosis
options.rationale: Hemarthrosis causes joint pain and swelling, not headache and vomiting.

questions.explanation: Intracranial bleeding is a medical emergency in hemophilia. Give factor replacement before imaging when a significant head injury occurs, and monitor neurologic status closely.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old has mild hemophilia A. The provider prescribes desmopressin (DDAVP) before a dental extraction. How does this medication work?

options.text: It replaces the missing factor IX needed to form a stable clot.
options.rationale: DDAVP does not contain clotting factor and is not effective for hemophilia B.

options.text: It dissolves existing clots.
options.rationale: Desmopressin promotes clotting; it does not dissolve clots.

options.text: It releases stored factor VIII and von Willebrand factor.
options.rationale: Correct. Desmopressin, a synthetic vasopressin, increases factor VIII levels 3-4 fold in mild hemophilia A.

options.text: It increases platelet production in the bone marrow.
options.rationale: DDAVP does not stimulate the bone marrow.

questions.explanation: DDAVP (IV or intranasal) is used for mild hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease. Monitor for fluid retention and hyponatremia, so fluids may be restricted around dosing. Antifibrinolytics such as aminocaproic acid are often used for mouth bleeding.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a hospitalized 5-year-old with hemophilia B. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoid intramuscular injections whenever possible
options.rationale: IM injections can cause deep muscle hematomas; use the subcutaneous or IV route.

options.text: Take temperatures by the rectal route
options.rationale: Rectal temperatures can injure the mucosa and cause bleeding; use oral, axillary, or tympanic routes.

options.text: Apply pressure for at least 5 minutes after venipuncture
options.rationale: Prolonged pressure promotes hemostasis after needle sticks.

options.text: Use a soft toothbrush
options.rationale: A soft toothbrush prevents gum bleeding while maintaining good oral hygiene.

options.text: Give acetaminophen for mild pain
options.rationale: Acetaminophen does not affect platelet function and is safe.

options.text: Encourage use of a straight razor when older
options.rationale: An electric razor is recommended to prevent cuts.

questions.explanation: Bleeding precautions in hemophilia: no IM injections or rectal temps, no aspirin or NSAIDs, prolonged pressure after punctures, soft toothbrush, electric razor, and padded environment for toddlers.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with hemophilia A is learning to self-infuse factor VIII at home for a bleed. Place the steps in the correct order.

items.text: Recognize early signs of a bleed, such as tingling or warmth in a joint
Perform hand hygiene and gather supplies
Reconstitute the factor concentrate according to directions
Perform venipuncture and infuse the factor IV at the prescribed rate
Apply pressure to the site and record the date, dose, and reason in the infusion log

questions.explanation: School-age children can learn to self-infuse with supervision, promoting independence. Early recognition (aura, tingling, warmth) and prompt infusion limit joint damage. Records help the hemophilia team adjust prophylaxis.

questions.stem: The parents of a 10-year-old with hemophilia ask which activity is safest for their son. Which activity should the nurse recommend?

options.text: Football
options.rationale: Contact sports carry a high risk of serious bleeding and head injury.

options.text: Ice hockey
options.rationale: Ice hockey is a high-contact sport with risk of trauma.

options.text: Wrestling
options.rationale: Wrestling involves direct body contact and joint stress.

options.text: Swimming
options.rationale: Correct. Swimming strengthens muscles that support and protect joints with minimal risk of trauma.

questions.explanation: Regular noncontact exercise (swimming, biking with a helmet, walking, golf) strengthens muscles around joints and reduces bleeding. Contact sports such as football, hockey, and wrestling are discouraged.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the medication list of a 14-year-old with hemophilia A who reports a headache after a soccer practice without head injury. Which medication should the nurse question?

options.text: Ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 6 hours as needed
options.rationale: Correct. NSAIDs inhibit platelet aggregation and increase the risk of bleeding in hemophilia.

options.text: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours as needed
options.rationale: Acetaminophen does not affect platelets and is the preferred analgesic.

options.text: Factor VIII concentrate IV as needed for bleeds
options.rationale: Factor replacement is the standard treatment.

options.text: Emicizumab subcutaneously every week
options.rationale: Emicizumab is a prophylactic agent that mimics factor VIII and reduces bleeding episodes in hemophilia A.

questions.explanation: Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) in hemophilia. Teach families to read labels on over-the-counter products, which may contain aspirin or salicylates.

questions.stem: A nurse provides teaching to the parents of a 2-year-old newly diagnosed with severe hemophilia A. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "We'll get our son a medical alert bracelet."
options.rationale: This is correct. A medical ID alerts responders to the diagnosis in an emergency.

options.text: "We'll pad the corners of the coffee table and use knee pads when he is learning to climb."
options.rationale: This is correct. Safety proofing reduces injury in active toddlers.

options.text: "We'll give children's aspirin if he has a fever."
options.rationale: Correct choice, because this statement is wrong. Aspirin impairs platelet function and increases bleeding; acetaminophen is used instead.

options.text: "We'll make sure his dentist knows about the hemophilia."
options.rationale: This is correct. Dental procedures may require factor or antifibrinolytic therapy beforehand.

questions.explanation: Teaching: medical ID, home safety, recognize and treat bleeds early, avoid aspirin and NSAIDs, good dental hygiene, routine immunizations given subcutaneously when possible with pressure, and genetic counseling.

questions.stem: A nurse is evaluating outcomes for a 13-year-old with hemophilia A who was treated for a knee hemarthrosis. Which finding indicates that treatment was effective?

options.text: The adolescent reports pain of 6/10 and the knee remains warm.
options.rationale: Ongoing pain and warmth suggest continued bleeding or inflammation.

options.text: The PTT is unchanged from the value measured on admission.
options.rationale: Hemophilia causes a chronically prolonged PTT; the joint response is the meaningful outcome.

options.text: The adolescent needs crutches to avoid all movement for 2 weeks.
options.rationale: Prolonged immobility causes stiffness; gradual return to motion is the goal.

options.text: Knee swelling has decreased, and the knee bends with only mild discomfort.
options.rationale: Correct. Reduced swelling and improving range of motion show the bleed has stopped and the joint is recovering.

questions.explanation: Outcomes after a joint bleed include reduced pain and swelling, restored range of motion, and prevention of chronic arthropathy. Prophylactic factor infusions reduce the frequency of joint bleeds.
